question: What are good alternatives to Evernote for building a personal knowledge base?
answer:
If you’re looking to replace Evernote for a personal knowledge base (PKB), the best choice depends on whether you care most about networked notes, simplicity, privacy, collaboration, web clipping, or long-term ownership of your data.

Here are some of the strongest alternatives:

Best overall Evernote replacements
Tool	Best for	Why people switch from Evernote	Tradeoffs
Obsidian	Personal knowledge systems, Zettelkasten, research	Local Markdown files, backlinks, graph view, huge plugin ecosystem	Less polished for collaboration; setup takes time
Notion	All-in-one workspace	Notes + databases + projects + wikis	Cloud-only; less ideal for massive offline archives
OneNote	Traditional note-taking	Free, excellent handwriting support, good organization	Weaker linking/knowledge graph features
Joplin	Privacy-focused Evernote-like experience	Open source, Markdown-based, encryption, syncing options	Interface is less refined
Logseq	Outliner-style thinking	Daily notes, backlinks, knowledge graphs	Smaller ecosystem; workflow is opinionated
Bear	Apple users who want simplicity	Beautiful writing experience, tags, Markdown export	Apple-only; less powerful for complex PKBs
Roam Research	Networked thinking	Popularized bidirectional linking	Expensive; cloud-based; less flexible storage
My recommendations by use case
1. You want a true “second brain”

Choose: Obsidian

Good if you want to collect:

Articles and research
Book notes
Ideas
Meeting notes
Personal documentation
Learning notes

Strengths:

Notes are plain Markdown files you own
Backlinks let ideas connect naturally
Thousands of community plugins
Works well for years of accumulated knowledge

A typical structure:

00 Inbox
01 Projects
02 Areas
03 Resources
04 Archive


Then link notes together rather than relying only on folders.

2. You want Evernote’s convenience plus organization

Choose: Notion

Good if your knowledge base includes:

Tasks
Databases
Reading lists
Personal CRM
Project planning

Example:

A “Books” database
A “People” database
A “Research” wiki
A daily journal

The downside is that very large collections can feel slower, and your data lives primarily in their ecosystem.

3. You want ownership and longevity

Choose: Obsidian or Joplin

These are better if you care about:

Exporting everything
Avoiding vendor lock-in
Keeping your archive readable decades later

Obsidian uses Markdown files directly. Joplin uses an open-source format and supports encrypted syncing.

4. You take lots of handwritten notes

Choose: OneNote

Especially good for:

Tablets
Stylus input
PDFs
Lecture notes
Sketches

It feels closer to a digital notebook than a knowledge graph.

5. You like daily journaling and thinking in outlines

Choose: Logseq

A common workflow:

Open today’s journal
Write everything there
Link concepts as they appear
Let connections emerge over time

It’s especially popular among people who think in bullet points.

If you are migrating from Evernote

A practical migration path:

Export Evernote notes (ENEX format).
Import into your chosen tool:
Obsidian: use an importer plugin or convert to Markdown
Joplin: direct Evernote import support
Notion: use Evernote import tools
Clean up:
Remove duplicate tags
Merge notebooks into broader categories
Add links between important notes

Avoid recreating Evernote’s notebook hierarchy exactly. PKBs tend to work better with:

fewer folders
better search
tags
links between concepts
My short list
Most people: Obsidian
Best all-in-one workspace: Notion
Best private/open-source option: Joplin
Best for handwriting: OneNote
Best for Apple simplicity: Bear
Best for “thinking out loud”: Logseq

If you tell me how you currently use Evernote (web clipping, PDFs, journaling, research, work notes, recipes, etc.), I can narrow this down to 1–2 options.

question: Is Obsidian free for personal and commercial use, and what do Sync and Publish add?
answer:
Yes. Obsidian is free for both personal and commercial use. You can download and use the app without paying, without creating an account, and without buying a license. The optional paid offerings are mainly services and support options. 
O
Obsidian
+1

What the free version includes

The free Obsidian app gives you the core knowledge-management features:

Unlimited notes (stored as local Markdown files)
Internal links and backlinks
Graph view
Plugins and themes
Offline use
Use at work, in a business, school, nonprofit, or personal project 
O
Obsidian

Your notes are stored locally on your device by default, rather than being stored in Obsidian’s cloud. 
O
Obsidian

What Obsidian Sync adds

Obsidian Sync is an optional paid service for keeping your vaults synchronized across devices. 
O
Obsidian

It adds:

Automatic syncing between computers and mobile devices
End-to-end encryption
Version history (restore older versions of notes)
Shared vault collaboration features
Priority support 
O
Obsidian

Pricing listed by Obsidian is:

$4 USD/user/month billed annually
$5 USD/user/month billed monthly 
O
Obsidian

You do not need Sync to use Obsidian. Many people use alternatives such as their own cloud storage or file-sync tools, though those approaches may require more setup. 
O
Obsidian Forum

What Obsidian Publish adds

Obsidian Publish lets you turn your notes into a website. 
O
Obsidian

It adds:

Publishing notes to the web
A hosted site (no server setup required)
Customizable themes
Graph view and full-text search for visitors
Priority support 
O
Obsidian

Pricing listed by Obsidian is:

$8 USD/site/month billed annually
$10 USD/site/month billed monthly 
O
Obsidian
What about the Commercial license?

The old distinction has changed: a Commercial license is now optional. Organizations can use Obsidian for work without buying one. The optional Commercial license ($50/user/year) is mainly a way for companies to support Obsidian’s development and be recognized as supporters. 
O
Obsidian
+1

A simple way to think about it:

Feature	Free Obsidian	Sync	Publish
Write and organize notes	✅	✅	✅
Local Markdown files	✅	✅	✅
Use commercially	✅	✅	✅
Sync devices automatically	❌	✅	❌
Encrypted Obsidian-managed sync	❌	✅	❌
Publish notes as a website	❌	❌	✅

For most individual users, the free version is enough. Sync is mainly worth it if you want a seamless multi-device setup, and Publish is for people who want to turn their notes into a public knowledge base, documentation site, or personal wiki.
